item.title: ToxicPanda Android malware uses VPN permissions to block Google Play
item.description: A banking trojan abuses Android's VPN permission model to cut off Play Store access and block security updates on infected devices.

item.title: Hackers infect Android car head units with proxy botnet malware
item.description: Compromised Android-based car infotainment units are being recruited into a residential-proxy botnet, widening the attack surface past phones and TVs.

item.title: TikTok Agrees to $400 Million Settlement in U.S. Child Privacy Lawsuit
item.description: TikTok settles a US child-privacy suit for $400M, the latest COPPA enforcement action against a social platform.

item.title: Double Fine confirms it owns all its games' IP and publishing rights after Xbox split
item.description: Double Fine now fully owns its catalog post-Xbox split, a rare case of a studio regaining control after an acquisition.

item.title: Compulsion Games' buyout is complete, so now Microsoft won't get a cut if you buy South of Midnight
item.description: Compulsion Games completed its independence buyout from Microsoft, so Xbox no longer takes a cut of South of Midnight sales.

item.title: Oldest human brain cells grown in lab 'recorded passage of time'
item.description: Lab-grown human brain cells retained a molecular record of elapsed time, hinting at how tissue age is tracked outside the body.

item.title: The superconducting gap of an ultrathin nickelate defies expectations
item.description:
Problem: Bilayer nickelate superconductors were discovered recently, but it wasn't clear whether they pair electrons the same way cuprate superconductors do, or whether a specific electron band even crosses the energy level that matters for conduction.
Approach, in plain words: Researchers grew strained thin films of a nickel-oxide compound and used a synchrotron light technique to directly image how electrons' energies are arranged in the material, then compared the results to theoretical predictions.
Result: The superconducting gap stays open in every direction, unlike cuprates' gap, which vanishes along certain directions. A band some theories expected to conduct actually sits below the conducting threshold, held there by strain in the crystal.
Why it matters: Confirms nickelates use a different pairing mechanism than cuprates, narrowing which theories of high-temperature superconductivity can be right.
Jargon glossary: - Fermi level: the energy threshold below which electron states are filled; only electrons near it conduct. - ARPES: a technique that fires light at a material and measures ejected electrons to map their energies. - d-wave pairing: a way of pairing electrons where the resulting gap vanishes along diagonal directions. - Epitaxial strain: stretching or compressing a thin film's crystal lattice to match the material it's grown on.

item.title: Making LEDs in the Home Fab
item.description:
Problem: Hobbyist chip fabrication has mostly stopped at proof-of-concept test structures; actually building and mounting a working, packaged LED chip is a harder wall.
Approach, in plain words: Starting from a raw gallium-nitride wafer, a UV laser cut through layers to expose contacts and slice out individual chips. Metal contacts were sputtered on through a stencil mask, then each chip was bonded to a circuit board using melted indium bumps, with a phosphor coating added to convert blue light to white.
Result: Functional blue and phosphor-converted white LEDs, soldered onto a real PCB rather than left as bare die on a bench.
Why it matters: Packaging and mounting a chip, not just fabricating it, has been the harder barrier for amateur semiconductor work — this build clears it.
Jargon glossary: - Epiwafer: a wafer with thin, precisely grown semiconductor layers on top. - Sputtering: depositing a thin metal film by knocking atoms off a target with ions. - Phosphor: a material that absorbs light at one color and re-emits it at another. - Bump bonding: connecting a chip to a board via small solder or metal bumps instead of wires.
